Recognizable by its tufted ears, the elusive lynx stalks snowshoe hares in winter.
Thick padded paws allow the solitary lynx to walk silently across deep snow.
Camouflaged among green leaves, the praying mantis folded its front legs waiting patiently.
With lightning speed, the predatory mantis lashed out to snatch a passing fly.
A vigilant meerkat stood upright on its hind legs scanning the desert sky.
When an eagle appeared, the sentry meerkat barked loudly to warn its burrow.
The sleek, dark-furred mink dove into the icy stream to catch crayfish.
Prized for its luxurious waterproof coat, the semiaquatic mink nests along wooded riverbanks.
Using broad spade-like paws, the subterranean mole dug fresh tunnels beneath our lawn.
Nearly blind, the velvety mole relies on sensitive whiskers to locate underground earthworms.
The agile mongoose darted sideways to dodge the venomous strike of a cobra.
Thick fur and quick reflexes protect the fearless mongoose when hunting deadly snakes.
A towering bull moose waded into the northern lake to feed on lilies.
Crowned with massive palmate antlers, the heavy moose browsed twigs in the forest.
Each dark-shelled mussel anchored itself tightly to the wave-battered coastal rocks with threads.
As a filter feeder, the freshwater mussel cleanses murky river water every day.
The small amphibious newt crawled from the mossy pond onto a damp log.
Bright orange skin warns predators that this woodland newt secretes dangerous skin toxins.
Startled by headlights, the nocturnal opossum collapsed and played dead beside the fence.
The mother opossum carried her tiny offspring safely inside her warm abdominal pouch.
With long reddish arms, the intelligent orangutan swung effortlessly through Bornean rainforest canopies.
The solitary orangutan fashioned a leafy umbrella to shelter itself from tropical rain.
Although flightless, the giant ostrich sprints across open plains faster than most horses.
Laying the largest eggs of any bird, the tall ostrich guards its nest.
Inside its rough calcified shell, the coastal oyster slowly formed a lustrous pearl.
Diners pried open the fresh saltwater oyster and served it raw on ice.
Cloaked in glossy black fur, the stealthy panther blended into the midnight jungle.
From a high branch, the muscular panther waited silently to pounce on deer.
To court a mate, the vibrant peacock unfurled its iridescent fan of feathers.
Dozens of shimmering eyespots decorated the extravagant train of the strutting male peacock.
The coastal pelican scooped gallons of seawater and fish into its expandable throat pouch.
Gliding low over ocean waves, the broad-winged pelican plunged down to catch mullet.
With a duck-like bill and webbed feet, the Australian platypus is an unusual mammal.
Unlike almost all other mammals, the venomous river-dwelling platypus lays leathery eggs.
When threatened by predators, the slow-moving porcupine raises its coat of sharp quills.
A foolish coyote retreated whimpering after barbed quills from the porcupine pierced its nose.
The massive nonvenomous python coiled tightly around its prey to suffocate it completely.
After swallowing a whole antelope, the heavy python rested motionless for two weeks.
Coiled beneath a desert rock, the venomous rattlesnake shook its tail in warning.
Hikers froze when they heard the dry buzzing sound of a hidden rattlesnake.
Herds of migratory reindeer trekked across the frozen Arctic tundra seeking winter lichen.
Both male and female reindeer grow branching antlers to dig through deep snow.
A cheerful red-breasted robin hopped across the dewy spring lawn pulling up earthworms.
Inside the blossoming apple tree, the songbird robin laid four bright blue eggs.
At first light, the proud barnyard rooster crowed loudly from atop the fence.
With a bright red comb, the territorial rooster strutted among the pecking hens.
Beneath the rotting forest log, a moist-skinned salamander hid from the drying sun.
Remarkably, an injured salamander can regenerate lost limbs and damaged tail tissue completely.
Driven by instinct, spawning salmon leap upstream over raging waterfalls to lay eggs.
Grizzly bears gathered at the river rapids to catch migrating silver salmon.
The nocturnal desert scorpion arched its segmented tail, readying its venomous stinger.
Using strong front pincers, the armored scorpion seized a cricket in the sand.
A noisy white seagull swooped down to snatch a french fry from beachgoers.
Riding the coastal updrafts, the scavenging seagull circled above the returning fishing boats.
The tiny upright seahorse anchored its curly tail around a swaying seagrass blade.
Uniquely among marine fish, the male seahorse incubates fertilized eggs inside his pouch.
Because of its frantic metabolism, the tiny insect-eating shrew must feed every few hours.
Mistaken for a mouse, the sharp-snouted shrew darted beneath the dry forest leaves.
The slow-moving sloth hangs upside down from rainforest canopy branches using curved claws.
Algae grows on the furry sloth because the arboreal mammal barely moves daily.
A small brown sparrow hopped along the sidewalk, pecking at scattered bread crumbs.
The common house sparrow builds its messy nest inside urban roofs and trees.
The deep-sea squid ejected a dark cloud of ink to escape hungry predators.
Using ten muscular tentacles, the fast-swimming squid captured a small fish at night.
A five-armed starfish clung tightly to the tide pool rock with tube feet.
Remarkably, an injured starfish can regenerate a completely new limb after losing one.
The flat-bodied stingray glided across the sandy ocean floor, hiding its venomous tail.
Swimmers shuffle their feet in shallow water to avoid stepping on a stingray.
A long-legged stork waded through the shallow marsh to catch frogs with its beak.
The white stork constructed a massive stick nest atop the tall village chimney.
The large, hairy tarantula ambushed a cricket outside its silk-lined desert burrow.
Despite its intimidating size, the venomous tarantula rarely bites humans unless provoked.
A colony of wood-eating termite workers silently hollowed out the old oak beams.
The subterranean termite digests tough plant cellulose with the help of gut microbes.
After hiking through tall grass, he found a blood-sucking tick embedded in skin.
The tiny parasitic tick can transmit Lyme disease while feeding on woodland mammals.
Unlike smooth-skinned frogs, the warty toad prefers dry gardens over wet ponds.
A nocturnal toad hopped across the damp patio to catch passing beetles.
The speckled rainbow trout swam upstream against the cold, rushing mountain river current.
Anglers cast artificial flies into clear freshwater streams to catch an elusive trout.
The sleek bluefin tuna is a fast oceanic predator prized for sushi.
Schools of large tuna migrate thousands of miles across the open Atlantic Ocean.
The coiled pit viper struck quickly, injecting potent venom through long hollow fangs.
Camouflaged among dead leaves, the ambush viper waited patiently for a warm-blooded rodent.
A bald-headed vulture circled high on thermal winds, searching for carrion below.
As nature's cleanup crew, the scavenging vulture feeds exclusively on dead animal carcasses.
Resembling a miniature kangaroo, the shy wallaby hopped through the Australian eucalyptus forest.
The mother wallaby carried her tiny joey safely inside a warm abdominal pouch.
Unlike a honeybee, the aggressive paper wasp can sting a threat multiple times.
A predatory wasp paralyzed the caterpillar and carried it back to its nest.
With its long, slender body, the agile weasel pursued mice into narrow burrows.
In northern climates, the carnivorous weasel molts its brown coat into white fur.
The stocky, muscular wolverine is a fierce arctic carnivore capable of fighting wolves.
Equipped with powerful jaws, a hungry wolverine can crush frozen bones in winter.
A red-headed woodpecker drummed rapidly against the dead tree trunk to find beetles.
Reinforced skull bones protect the chiseling woodpecker from brain injury while hammering wood.
The nocturnal aardvark uses its powerful, shovel-like claws to excavate hardened termite mounds across the African savanna.
Equipped with a long, sticky tongue, the burrowing aardvark can consume tens of thousands of insects in a single night.
As a vital rainforest seed disperser, the agouti is one of the few rodents with teeth strong enough to gnaw through tough Brazil nut pods.
The fleet-footed agouti buries surplus nuts across the forest floor, inadvertently cultivating the next generation of canopy trees.
Boasting the longest wingspan of any extant bird, the wandering albatross can glide effortlessly across oceanic wind currents for thousands of miles.
The pelagic albatross spends most of its life over the open sea, returning to remote subantarctic islands only to breed.
Rather than relying on venom, the massive green anaconda subdues its prey in South American swamps through powerful muscular constriction.
With eyes and nostrils positioned atop its head, the semiaquatic anaconda can stalk unsuspecting capybaras while remaining almost entirely submerged.
In the pitch-black abyssal zone, the deep-sea anglerfish dangles a bioluminescent lure from its forehead to attract curious prey.
Extreme sexual dimorphism characterizes certain anglerfish species, wherein the diminutive male permanently fuses to the much larger female.
Gardeners frequently introduce ladybugs to control the sap-sucking aphid, which can rapidly defoliate ornamental rose bushes.
Ants often tend colonies of the tiny aphid like livestock, protecting the soft-bodied insects in exchange for their sugary honeydew secretions.
Unlike most amphibians that undergo metamorphosis, the neotenic axolotl retains its feathery external gills and aquatic lifestyle throughout adulthood.
Medical researchers study the critically endangered axolotl for its extraordinary ability to regenerate severed limbs, spinal cords, and cardiac tissue.
Native to the Indonesian islands, the male babirusa is a wild swine renowned for upper canines that pierce right through the top of its snout.
If a male babirusa fails to grind down its continuously growing tusks, the curving teeth can eventually arch backward and penetrate its own skull.
Foraging across the Australian bush at dusk, the pointy-snouted bandicoot leaves distinctive conical pits in the soil as it digs for subterranean fungi and grubs.
Although roughly the size of a rabbit, the nocturnal bandicoot is an omnivorous marsupial with a rear-opening pouch that protects its developing young from dirt while burrowing.
Once a free-swimming larva, the adult barnacle secretes a remarkably resilient calcium plate and cements itself permanently to ship hulls, pier pilings, or whale skin.
When the tide comes in, the sessile barnacle extends its feathery cirri from its shell to filter microscopic plankton from the turbulent coastal water.
Built like a silver torpedo with a jutting underbite of razor-sharp teeth, the predatory barracuda ambushes reef fish with explosive bursts of speed.
Divers near tropical coral reefs often observe the solitary barracuda hovering motionless in the water column before striking at flashing schools of baitfish.
Adapted to life amid shifting Arctic sea ice, the white beluga lacks a dorsal fin and possesses a flexible, bulbous forehead called a melon used for echolocation.
Early mariners dubbed the gregarious beluga the 'canary of the sea' because of its extensive repertoire of high-pitched clicks, whistles, and trills.
Moving deliberately through the Southeast Asian canopy, the shaggy binturong uses its muscular, prehensile tail as a fifth limb to grip branches.
Often called the bearcat, the arboreal binturong emits a distinctive musk from its scent glands that smells unmistakably like hot buttered popcorn.
Despite its serpentine appearance, the burrowing blindworm is actually a legless lizard equipped with functional eyelids and a detachable tail.
Gardeners turning over damp compost heaps in European woodlands occasionally uncover a bronze-colored blindworm hunting for slugs and earthworms.
Endemic to the dense forests south of the Congo River, the matriarchal bonobo is one of humankind's closest living genetic relatives.
Unlike the more aggressive common chimpanzee, the egalitarian bonobo frequently resolves social tension and troop conflict through affiliative grooming and peaceful cooperation.
Resembling a large, segmented earthworm, the subterranean caecilian is a limbless tropical amphibian that navigates moist soil using sensory tentacles on its snout.
Because the elusive caecilian spends almost its entire life burrowing beneath leaf litter and mud, herpetologists still know relatively little about its natural population density.
Cruising silently through the flooded Amazon basin, the spectacled caiman is a scaly crocodilian named for the bony ridge connecting its eye sockets.
Though generally smaller than the American alligator, the black caiman serves as a formidable apex predator in slow-moving South American river systems.
Weighing over one hundred pounds, the barrel-bodied capybara is the world's largest extant rodent and thrives in large social groups along South American riverbanks.
With partially webbed feet and high-set eyes, the herbivorous capybara readily retreats into the water to evade prowling jaguars and anacondas.
Instantly recognizable by its long, black-tufted ears, the agile caracal is a medium-sized wild cat native to the arid savannas of Africa and the Middle East.
Driven by powerful hind legs, a hunting caracal can leap nearly ten feet into the air to swat low-flying birds right out of the sky.
Topped with a tall, keratinous casque on its head, the flightless cassowary strides through the rainforests of New Guinea and northeastern Australia.
When cornered, the territorial cassowary can deliver a lethal kick using the dagger-like, five-inch claw on its inner toe.
Unlike the herbivorous millipede, the fast-moving centipede is a venomous arthropod predator that subdues insects and small vertebrates using modified front legs called forcipules.
Each body segment of a desert centipede bears a single pair of legs, allowing it to dart rapidly beneath rocks and decaying logs in search of prey.
Equipped with elastic, padded hooves, the sure-footed chamois navigates sheer alpine precipices across the rugged mountain ranges of Europe.
Before synthetic microfibers were invented, the supple hide of the mountain-dwelling chamois was prized for crafting ultra-soft polishing cloths.
To survive the freezing temperatures of the high Andes, the crepuscular chinchilla possesses the densest fur of any land mammal, sprouting dozens of hairs from each follicle.
Because water trapped in its thick coat could cause fatal hypothermia or fungal growth, a chinchilla cleans itself by rolling vigorously in fine volcanic dust.
After spending up to seventeen years underground feeding on xylem sap, the periodical cicada emerges in synchronized millions to molt and mate in the treetops.
On sweltering summer afternoons, the male cicada vibrates specialized drum-like organs called tymbals on its abdomen to produce a deafening mating chorus.
Nocturnal and sleek-bodied, Asian palm civets play a peculiar role in luxury agriculture by eating and fermenting ripe coffee cherries in their digestive tracts.
Resembling long-nosed cats with banded tails, solitary civets mark their woodland territories across Africa and Asia using potent perineal scent glands.
Holding its ringed tail upright like a beacon in the tall grass, the diurnal coati travels in noisy bands while poking its flexible snout into crevices for beetles and fruit.
A South American relative of the raccoon, the agile coati possesses reversible ankles that allow it to descend tree trunks headfirst with ease.
Long presumed extinct since the end of the Cretaceous period, a living coelacanth was famously discovered in 1938 off the coast of South Africa.
The deep-dwelling coelacanth is a lobe-finned fish whose fleshy, limb-like fins offer evolutionary biologists critical insight into how ancient vertebrates first transitioned onto land.
Soaring on thermal updrafts high above the Andean peaks, the giant condor scans the barren landscape for carrion using its keen eyesight.
The bald head of the scavenging condor is an evolutionary adaptation that prevents feathers from becoming matted with blood while feeding inside large carcasses.
By rapidly expanding and contracting millions of pigmented chromatophores in its skin, the intelligent cuttlefish can camouflage itself against any seabed texture in milliseconds.
Unlike squids, the cephalopod cuttlefish regulates its buoyancy using a porous, internal calcium carbonate shell known as a cuttlebone.
Closely related to the manatee, the gentle dugong grazes exclusively on underwater seagrass meadows in the warm coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific.
Distinguished from other sirenians by its notched, whale-like tail fluke and downturned snout, the herbivorous dugong inspired ancient sailor legends of mermaids.
Despite the persistent folklore that it crawls into human ears, the nocturnal earwig is a harmless omnivorous insect that uses its rear pincers for defense and folding its delicate wings.
Unusual among non-social insects, the female earwig exhibits dedicated maternal care by guarding, cleaning, and feeding her clutch of eggs until the nymphs hatch.
Covered in coarse hair and protective keratin spines, the short-beaked echidna is an Australian monotreme that reproduces by laying leathery eggs rather than giving live birth.
Like its aquatic cousin the platypus, the burrowing echidna uses electroreceptors in its elongated snout to detect the faint electrical signals of subterranean ants and termites.
Looking like a slender cross between a cougar and a mongoose, the agile fossa is the largest mammalian carnivore endemic to the island of Madagascar.
Equipped with semi-retractable claws and a long balancing tail, the predatory fossa relentlessly pursues lemurs through the highest branches of the forest canopy.
With its spotted coat, ringed tail, and elongated body, the nocturnal genet is frequently mistaken for a small wild cat as it stalks rodents through African scrublands.
Agile enough to squeeze through any opening wider than its skull, the solitary genet hunts insects, reptiles, and roosting birds under the cover of darkness.

Critically endangered and native to the river systems of the Indian subcontinent, the fish-eating gharial is immediately identifiable by its exceptionally long, narrow snout lined with interlocking teeth.
Mature male gharials develop a hollow, bulbous nasal growth at the tip of their snout that resembles an earthen pot and acts as a vocal resonator to produce buzzing mating calls.
The agile gibbon swung effortlessly through the dense rainforest canopy using its remarkably long arms.
Early in the morning, the loud, melodic calls of the gibbon echoed across the tropical valley to establish its territory.
During the annual migration, thousands of bearded gnu thundered across the dusty African plains in search of fresh pasture.
Also known as a wildebeest, the gnu is a large antelope with curved horns and a distinctive ox-like build.
The wild guanaco grazed peacefully on the arid slopes of the Andes Mountains, well adapted to the thin, high-altitude air.
Closely related to the domesticated llama, the slender guanaco has thick, reddish-brown wool that protects it from freezing winds.
The prehistoric-looking hoatzin is famous for its spiky crest and its unique digestive system that ferments leaves like a cow.
A newly hatched hoatzin possesses tiny claws on its wing digits, allowing the young bird to climb through swamp branches before it can fly.
The sure-footed ibex scaled the nearly vertical cliff face with astonishing balance, using its specialized hooves to grip narrow ledges.
With its magnificent, backward-curving ridged horns, the male ibex stood silhouetted against the snowy alpine peak.
Startled by a stalking leopard, the graceful impala leaped nearly ten feet into the air to confuse the predator and escape into the brush.
A herd of reddish-brown impala gathered cautiously at the edge of the watering hole, their slender legs tensed for sudden flight.
The tiny desert jerboa hopped rapidly across the hot sand dunes on its elongated, kangaroo-like hind legs.
Using its long, tufted tail for balance, the nocturnal jerboa can make sharp, erratic leaps to evade hungry owls in the dark.
Perched motionless on a willow branch overhanging the stream, the vibrant blue kingfisher waited patiently for a minnow to swim near the surface.
With a sudden, dagger-like dive into the clear water, the kingfisher captured a small fish in its long, pointed bill.
The nocturnal kinkajou used its prehensile tail to hang securely from a high branch while reaching for ripe figs in the rainforest canopy.
Often called a honey bear because of its fondness for sweet nectar, the golden-furred kinkajou is actually a tropical relative of the raccoon.
Native to New Zealand, the flightless kiwi forages on the forest floor at night, using nostrils at the tip of its long beak to sniff out earthworms.
Covered in hair-like feathers and lacking a visible tail, the shy kiwi lays one of the largest eggs in proportion to its body size of any bird.
The loud, echoing call of the Australian kookaburra sounds remarkably like boisterous human laughter ringing through the eucalyptus trees.
As a large terrestrial kingfisher, the kookaburra hunts lizards, insects, and small snakes rather than diving for fish in rivers.
Massive swarms of tiny, shrimp-like krill turn the frigid Southern Ocean waters pink and serve as the primary food source for baleen whales.
Although each individual krill is only a few centimeters long, these small crustaceans form the vital foundation of the Antarctic marine food web.
The male kudu blended seamlessly into the thorny woodland, its vertical white body stripes and long, spiraling horns camouflaged among the branches.
Despite its large size, the shy kudu can clear high bush fences with a single effortless bound when threatened by predators.
Beneath the deep winter snowpack of the Arctic tundra, the small, thick-furred lemming tunneled tirelessly in search of mosses and grasses.
Population booms among the Tundra lemming directly influence the breeding success of snowy owls and arctic foxes that depend on the rodent for food.
In the snowy mountains of Japan, a troop of furry macaque monkeys soaked together in a natural volcanic hot spring to stay warm.
The resourceful macaque used a flat stone to crack open hard nuts, demonstrating the complex social intelligence typical of Old World monkeys.
Recognizable by its striking black-and-white plumage and long tail, the intelligent magpie is a member of the crow family known for its complex vocalizations.
A curious magpie hopped across the garden lawn, tilting its head as it searched for beetles and fallen seeds.
The black mamba is one of Africa's most feared venomous snakes, capable of moving at remarkable speeds when cornered in the savanna scrub.
Named for the dark interior of its mouth rather than its olive-gray scales, the mamba displays an intimidating threat posture when startled.
Often referred to as a sea cow, the gentle manatee glided slowly through the warm coastal lagoon while grazing on underwater seagrass.
Using its paddle-shaped tail and front flippers, the hefty manatee surfaced quietly to take a breath of air before submerging again.
With brilliant blue and red ridges on its snout and a golden beard, the dominant male mandrill is the most colorful primate in the equatorial rainforest.
As the largest species of monkey in the world, the stocky mandrill spends much of its day foraging in large troops along the jungle floor.
Standing upright on a sun-warmed boulder, the plump alpine marmot let out a piercing whistle to warn its colony of a circling golden eagle.
After spending the brief mountain summer building up a thick layer of fat, the marmot retreats into a deep underground burrow to hibernate for seven months.
The slow-moving millipede rippled across the damp forest floor, coordinating dozens of pairs of tiny legs as it fed on decaying leaves.
When disturbed by a curious bird, the armored millipede immediately curled into a tight spiral to protect its soft underside.
Swimming beneath the shifting pack ice of the Arctic Ocean, the male narwhal is easily identified by the long, spiraled tusk protruding from its upper jaw.
Scientists discovered that the iconic tusk of the narwhal is actually an elongated, sensitive tooth containing millions of nerve endings.
Considered a living fossil, the chambered nautilus regulates its buoyancy in the deep ocean by pumping gas and water through its coiled, pearly shell.
At night, the ancient nautilus ascends toward shallower coral reefs, propelling itself backward with jets of water expelled from its funnel.
Hidden deep within the dense hawthorn thicket, the plain brown nightingale filled the evening air with a rich, extraordinarily varied song.
Poets have long celebrated the nightingale for its habit of singing complex, flute-like melodies well after twilight has fallen.
Using its long, sticky tongue, the striped numbat extracted hundreds of termites from a rotting eucalyptus log in the Western Australian bush.
Unlike most other marsupials, the endangered numbat is active exclusively during the day so it can match the activity cycle of its termite prey.
Moving silently through the tangled undergrowth, the nocturnal ocelot relied on its dappled, rosette-patterned coat to remain invisible to prey.
Roughly twice the size of a domestic house cat, the sleek ocelot is an agile climber and swimmer native to the tropical forests of the Americas.
Although its zebra-striped hindquarters suggest otherwise, the elusive forest okapi is actually the only living relative of the giraffe.
The solitary okapi used its long, prehensile blue tongue to strip fresh buds and leaves from low-hanging branches in the dense Congolese rainforest.
With its striking black-and-white facial markings and long, rapier-straight horns, the desert oryx stood resiliently against the blistering sandstorm.
Adapted to survive in extreme heat without drinking water for weeks, the oryx obtains moisture directly from desert melons and sparse roots.
Covered from head to tail in overlapping keratin scales, the shy pangolin rolled into an impenetrable ball when approached by a prowling lion.
As the world's only truly scaly mammal, the nocturnal pangolin uses its powerful front claws to tear open hard termite mounds.
A noisy herd of collared peccary rooted through the dry desert scrub, using their tough, disk-shaped snouts to dig up succulent bulbs and prickly pear cacti.
Though it closely resembles a small wild boar, the peccary belongs to a distinct New World family characterized by downward-pointing, interlocking tusks.
Equipped with interlocking, razor-sharp triangular teeth and powerful jaws, the red-bellied piranha can shear through tough flesh in seconds.
In the murky waters of the Amazon River basin, a school of piranha darted rapidly toward the splashes of an injured fish.
As winter arrived on the windswept tundra, the brown plumage of the ptarmigan molted into pure white feathers, rendering the bird nearly invisible against the snow.
Dense feathers covering the feet of the hardy ptarmigan act like natural snowshoes, allowing the grouse to walk easily across soft drifts.
High in the misty cloud forests of Central America, the male resplendent quetzal displayed its iridescent emerald plumage and streaming twin tail feathers.
Revered by ancient Maya and Aztec civilizations, the colorful quetzal feeds primarily on wild avocados, swallowing the fruit whole before regurgitating the pit.
Famous for its cheerful, smiling facial expression, the small, herbivorous quokka hopped inquisitively through the coastal shrubland of Rottnest Island.
Like its larger cousin the kangaroo, the nocturnal quokka is a marsupial that carries its developing young in a protective front pouch.
With the longest legs and largest ears relative to body size of any cat, the spotted serval can detect the faint rustle of rodents hidden deep in tall savanna grass.
The slender serval leaped straight into the air and pinned a fleeing guinea fowl with a swift, precise strike of its front paws.
The shoebill is a large, stork-like wading bird native to East African swamps, immediately recognizable by its massive, clog-shaped beak.
Standing motionless in the papyrus marshes, the shoebill ambushes lungfish and small crocodiles with a sudden, forceful strike.
Thousands of starlings wheeled across the twilight sky in a synchronized aerial display known as a murmuration.
With its iridescent dark plumage and remarkable talent for vocal mimicry, the starling can imitate everything from rival bird calls to mechanical alarms.
Often referred to as a living fossil, the armored sturgeon has patrolled northern rivers and coastal waters since the age of the dinosaurs.
Overfishing and dam construction have severely depleted wild sturgeon populations, which have long been prized as the primary source of true caviar.
Inhabiting the arid heart of Australia, the inland taipan possesses the most potent neurotoxic venom of any land snake in the world.
Despite its lethal reputation, the shy taipan typically avoids human contact and preys almost exclusively on native rodents.
Using its flexible, prehensile snout like a miniature trunk, the forest-dwelling tapir plucks tender leaves and fruit from low-hanging branches.
Although it superficially resembles a large pig, the tapir is actually an odd-toed ungulate closely related to horses and rhinoceroses.
Each of the nocturnal tarsier's enormous eyes is heavier than its brain, granting the tiny Southeast Asian primate exceptional night vision.
Clinging vertically to slender tree trunks, the carnivorous tarsier rotates its head nearly 180 degrees to locate insects before leaping to catch them.
The toucan's oversized, brightly colored bill is surprisingly lightweight because its interior consists of a spongy network of bony fibers.
Beyond helping the bird reach fruit on slender rainforest branches, the toucan's large beak radiates excess body heat to regulate its temperature.
Endemic to New Zealand, the tuatara looks like a lizard but belongs to an ancient reptilian order that flourished over 200 million years ago.
Scientists study the slow-growing tuatara for its unique evolutionary traits, including a light-sensitive third eye on the top of its skull.
Graceful herds of wild vicuna graze on the tough bunchgrasses of the high Andean plateaus at elevations above twelve thousand feet.
Once hunted nearly to extinction for its extraordinarily fine, warm undercoat, the vicuna is now strictly protected and shorn live by local communities.
Distinguished from a field mouse by its stouter body, rounded muzzle, and shorter tail, the meadow vole excavates intricate runways beneath the grass.
Because it reproduces rapidly and remains active beneath the winter snowpack, the herbivorous vole serves as a vital food source for owls and foxes.
When startled on the African savanna, the warthog sprints toward its burrow with its tufted tail held straight up like a flagpole.
The prominent facial pads that give the warthog its name are thick cartilaginous growths that cushion its skull during tusk-to-tusk combat.
Easily identified by its elongated, downward-curving snout, the boll weevil is a tiny beetle notorious for devastating cotton crops.
The female acorn weevil uses the chewing mouthparts at the tip of her long rostrum to drill a microscopic shaft into a nut before laying her eggs inside.
Every year, over a million wildebeests undertake a perilous circular migration across the Serengeti in pursuit of fresh grazing and seasonal rains.
With its boxy head, curved horns, and shaggy mane, the wildebeest is a large social antelope that forms the backbone of the East African grassland ecosystem.
Equipped with rodent-like incisors and powerful claws, the muscular wombat excavates extensive burrow systems across southeastern Australia.
The nocturnal wombat is a barrel-shaped marsupial with a backward-facing pouch that prevents soil from covering its young while digging.

She grated the fragrant yellow zest from the lemon peel into the cake batter.
Colorful citrus zest contains aromatic oils that add bright flavor without extra liquid.
Native to the Amazon rainforest, the abiu is a round yellow fruit prized for its translucent, caramel-flavored flesh.
You should wait until the abiu is completely ripe before eating it to avoid the sticky latex present in the skin of unripe specimens.
What most people think are the tiny seeds on the outside of a strawberry are actually individual dry fruits called achenes.
Botanically speaking, a sunflower seed is an achene because its hard outer shell does not split open on its own when ripe.
Although it is the national fruit of Jamaica, ackee must be allowed to split open naturally on the tree before harvesting to ensure the toxic compounds have dissipated.
When cooked with salted cod, the creamy yellow arils of the ackee fruit resemble scrambled eggs in both texture and appearance.
Cultivated primarily in southern Japan, the amanatsu is a yellowish-orange citrus fruit known for its refreshing, bittersweet flavor.
Because its thick rind is easy to peel by hand, the amanatsu is often enjoyed fresh or made into tangy summer marmalades.
The crunchy green flesh of an unripe ambarella is frequently sliced and tossed with chili salt as a popular street snack in Southeast Asia.
As the ambarella ripens to a golden yellow, its fibrous interior develops a tropical flavor reminiscent of pineapple and mango.
Also known as the Indian gooseberry, the small green amla fruit is exceptionally rich in vitamin C and has a sharp, astringent taste.
In traditional Ayurvedic practices, dried and powdered amla is used in both culinary chutneys and herbal tonics.
Closely related to the common guava, the Brazilian araça is a small, tart yellow berry that makes an aromatic tropical jam.
Because the delicate skin of the araça bruises easily after harvest, the fruit is rarely exported and is mostly consumed locally.
Often called chokeberries due to their mouth-puckering astringency when raw, dark purple aronia berries are packed with beneficial antioxidants.
Sweetening the tart juice of the aronia fruit makes it an excellent base for syrups, wines, and fruit jellies.
The atemoya is a deliberate hybrid between the sugar apple and the cherimoya, combining a bumpy green rind with custard-like sweet flesh.
Chilling a ripe atemoya before scooping out its creamy white pulp enhances its vanilla and tropical fruit notes.
Resembling a miniature crabapple, the Mediterranean azarole grows on a thorny hawthorn tree and carries a pleasant, tangy apple flavor.
In southern Europe, ripe red and yellow azarole fruits are traditionally simmered with sugar to make rustic preserves.
Beneath its thick, resinous rind, the Amazonian bacuri holds fragrant white pulp that is prized for making artisanal ice creams and sorbets.
Foragers collect the bacuri only after the heavy fruit naturally ripens and falls from the canopy to the forest floor.
The woody outer shell of the bael fruit is so hard that it must be cracked open with a hammer or machete to reach the aromatic orange pulp inside.
During scorching summer months in India, the sweet, mucilaginous flesh of the bael is blended with water and sugar to create a cooling beverage.
Unlike most fleshy fruits, the velvety pod of the African baobab tree dries directly on the branch, producing a tangy, chalky pulp.
The nutrient-dense powder extracted from the inside of a baobab fruit pod adds a bright, citrusy acidity to smoothies and baked goods.
Chinese bayberry, often marketed as yangmei, is a crimson fruit with a knobby, pebble-like surface and sweet-tart juice.
Because fresh bayberry has a very short shelf life, it is frequently preserved in syrup, dried as a snack, or fermented into liqueur.
The small, ovoid bibhitaki fruit is harvested from large deciduous trees in India and dried for use in traditional herbal formulations.
Along with amla and haritaki, the astringent bibhitaki fruit forms one-third of the famous Ayurvedic blend known as Triphala.
Growing in clusters directly from the tree trunk, the bright green bilimbi looks like a miniature cucumber but has an intensely sour, acidic flavor.
Filipino and Indonesian cooks often use sliced bilimbi as a tangy souring agent in fish stews and spicy relishes.
Covered in soft, flexible projections that turn yellow when ripe, the biriba is famous for having soft flesh that tastes remarkably like lemon meringue pie.
Because the tender skin of the biriba darkens and bruises swiftly after picking, it is best eaten fresh right beneath the tree.
The fruit of the buriti palm is encased in shiny, reddish-brown scales that protect a vibrant orange pulp rich in beta-carotene.
After soaking the scaly buriti fruit in warm water to soften its exterior, locals scrape off the oily flesh to make sweet pastes and juices.
The tiny calamansi citrus has a thin green rind and fragrant, sour orange flesh that combines the flavors of lime and tangerine.
Squeezing fresh calamansi juice over grilled seafood or stir-fried noodles is an essential finishing touch in Filipino cuisine.
When sliced horizontally, the ridged yellow carambola reveals a five-pointed star shape that gives the starfruit its common name.
The entire waxy carambola is edible, offering a crisp, juicy texture and a flavor that ranges from tart to mildly sweet.
Also called the Natal plum, the crimson carissa berry grows on a thorny coastal shrub and exudes a harmless white sap when picked.
When cooked with sugar, the cranberry-like tartness of the carissa transforms into a vibrant ruby-red jelly.
Closely related to the jackfruit, the tubular cempedak features softer, golden-yellow pods with a much stronger, musky aroma.
Once the spiky rind of a ripe cempedak is sliced open, you can pull the central core to extract all the sweet, custard-like fruit bulbs at once.
Resembling a large, round raspberry, the ripe red che fruit has a chewy texture and a mild flavor reminiscent of fresh figs and watermelon.
The hardy che tree belongs to the mulberry family and produces abundant clusters of sweet, maroon-colored aggregate fruits in late autumn.
Bananas, peaches, and avocados are classified as climacteric fruits because they continue to ripen and soften after being harvested from the plant.
Placing a climacteric fruit in a paper bag traps the ethylene gas it releases, which significantly speeds up the ripening process.
Native to the Andean foothills, the cocona is a close relative of the tomato that grows as a yellow-to-red berry with a bright, citrus-like acidity.
In the Amazon basin, peeled cocona fruit is blended with chili peppers and herbs to create a zesty table sauce.
Found along tropical beaches, the salt-tolerant cocoplum shrub bears small, round fruits with thin skin and cottony, sweet white flesh.
Inside the soft pulp of the cocoplum lies a ridged, edible seed that tastes surprisingly similar to a fresh almond.
Often called the mandarin melon berry, the fruit of the cudrania tree is a bumpy red sphere that softens and sweetens after the first autumn frost.
Gardeners prize the thorny cudrania for its pest-resistant fruit, which yields a richly flavored red pulp with tiny crunchable seeds.
A close relative of the cacao tree, the Amazonian cupuacu produces heavy brown pods filled with creamy, intensely fragrant white pulp.
While the tart flesh of the cupuacu is blended into juices and desserts, its fat-rich seeds can be pressed to make a white chocolate-like confection.
Recognizable by the prominent protruding bump at its stem end, the dekopon is a large, seedless mandarin hybrid prized for its exceptional sweetness.
Sold as Sumo Citrus in many grocery stores, the dekopon has a loose, pebbled orange skin that peels away effortlessly without leaving bitter pith behind.
In botany, a drupe is any fruit—such as a peach, cherry, or olive—in which soft outer flesh surrounds a single hard, woody pit.
Although many people think of a coconut or an almond as a nut, each is technically the seed or pit extracted from inside a fibrous drupe.
Growing in grape-like clusters on tropical trees, the buff-colored duku looks like a tiny potato on the outside but holds translucent, juicy segments inside.
When eating fresh duku, you should avoid biting into the green seeds, which are extremely bitter in contrast to the sweet, grapefruit-flavored flesh.
Fruits of the genus elaeagnus, such as the autumn olive and goumi berry, are covered in tiny silver scales and turn bright red when ripe.
Once fully ripened on the bush, elaeagnus berries lose their astringency and offer a sweet-tart flavor high in lycopene.
The pale green emblic fruit has crisp, sour flesh marked by six vertical stripes running from stem to tip.
After chewing a raw emblic, drinking plain water leaves a lingering sensation of sweetness on the palate due to the fruit's unique tannins.
The endocarp is the innermost layer of a fruit's wall, which directly surrounds and protects the developing seed.
In stone fruits like plums and apricots, the endocarp hardens into the woody pit, whereas in citrus fruits it forms the juicy segments we eat.
Acting as a protective barrier against pests and moisture loss, the exocarp is the outermost skin or peel of a fruit.
While the thin, smooth exocarp of an apple or grape is eaten right along with the flesh, the tough, leathery exocarp of a pomegranate is discarded.
The spiny orange gac fruit is prized in Vietnamese cuisine for its nutrient-dense red arils that impart a vibrant crimson color to glutinous rice.
Harvested from a perennial melon vine native to Southeast Asia, gac contains exceptionally high concentrations of beta-carotene and lycopene.
Street vendors across the Caribbean sell clusters of green-skinned genip, which consumers crack open with their teeth to suck on the tangy, salmon-colored pulp.
Although the leathery rind of the genip is inedible, the translucent flesh inside offers a refreshing blend of sweet and astringent flavors.
Permaculture gardeners value the goumi shrub not only for its nitrogen-fixing roots but also for its tart, silver-speckled red berries.
Once fully ripe in mid-summer, the astringency of the goumi fruit mellows into a pleasant flavor reminiscent of sour cherry and rhubarb.
Often called the Brazilian cherry, the dark purple grumichama features a tender skin and juicy pulp that tastes remarkably like a sweet Bing cherry.
Because the delicate grumichama bruises easily after harvest, this tropical myrtle fruit is rarely found in commercial markets outside of home orchards.
Despite its misleading name, the guavaberry is unrelated to the true guava and instead grows as a small, spicy-scented berry in Caribbean forests.
During the winter holidays in the Virgin Islands, locals steep wild-harvested guavaberry fruit in rum and spices to craft a traditional festive liqueur.
Foragers gather the tiny, dark purple hackberry in late autumn, enjoying its thin layer of date-sweet flesh along with its crunchy, edible seed.
Because dried hackberry fruits resist spoilage over long winters, they served as a reliable source of calories and calcium for prehistoric Indigenous peoples.
Revered in Ayurvedic medicine as a foundational healing tonic, the bitter and astringent haritaki fruit is typically dried and ground into a fine powder.
The ridged, olive-shaped haritaki drupe is combined with two other native Indian fruits to formulate the classic herbal remedy known as Triphala.
Native to Hiroshima Prefecture, the hassaku is a firm, yellow-orange citrus hybrid with a crisp texture and a balanced combination of sweetness and gentle bitterness.
To prepare a fresh hassaku for eating, one must peel away both the thick outer rind and the tough inner membranes surrounding each juicy segment.
Resembling miniature crabapples, bright red hawthorn berries hang on thorny hedgerows well into winter, providing vital sustenance for migrating thrushes.
In northern China, tart hawthorn fruits are skewered on bamboo sticks and dipped in hardened sugar syrup to create a popular street snack.
In botanical classification, any citrus fruit—from a tiny kumquat to a massive pomelo—is categorized as a hesperidium due to its leathery rind and segmented interior.
The tough outer peel of a hesperidium is dotted with aromatic oil glands that protect the fluid-filled vesicles inside from pests and dehydration.
Unlike most citrus varieties whose white pith is unpleasantly bitter, the pale yellow hyuganatsu is eaten with its fluffy inner rind intact to complement its tart juice.
Cultivated primarily in southern Japan, the fragrant hyuganatsu is sliced thinly in spiral ribbons and served with a light dusting of sugar.
Closely related to the cherimoya, the tropical ilama splits open when ripe to reveal either creamy white or rose-pink custard-like flesh.
Because the conical ilama fruit has a very brief shelf life once harvested from the lowlands of Central America, it remains a rare delicacy elsewhere.
Commonly referred to as wild mango or dika nut, the fibrous fruit of the West African irvingia tree encloses a fat-rich seed prized for thickening traditional soups.
While villagers snack on the sweet yellow pulp of ripe irvingia fruits, the commercial value of the harvest lies primarily in its nutritious kernels.
Second only to the mikan in Japanese citrus production, the bright orange iyokan is celebrated for its fragrant peel and exceptionally juicy, sweet-tart segments.
Because the rind of an iyokan is thicker than that of a standard mandarin, yet still easy to peel by hand, it ships well throughout the winter season.
The Brazilian jabuticaba is famous for its cauliflorous growth habit, in which glossy, purple-black fruits sprout directly from the trunk and main branches of the tree.
Beneath its tannic, thick skin, the grape-like jabuticaba holds a translucent white pulp that is eaten fresh or fermented into rich wines and jellies.
During the Indian monsoon season, vendors sell mounds of oblong, deep purple jamun fruit tossed with black salt to counterbalance its puckering astringency.
Eating fresh jamun leaves a telltale violet stain on the tongue and lips due to the high concentration of anthocyanin pigments in its skin.
Across Central America, the plum-sized jocote is enjoyed both in its crunchy, unripe green state with salt and lime, and when fully ripened to a sweet red.
A large, fibrous pit takes up most of the volume inside a jocote, leaving a thin layer of aromatic, yellow flesh beneath its smooth skin.
Harvested while its rind is still vibrant green, the sour Japanese kabosu citrus is squeezed over grilled fish and sashimi in place of lemon or vinegar.
Closely related to yuzu, the round kabosu lends a sharp, floral acidity to artisanal ponzu sauces and regional condiments in Oita Prefecture.
The drought-hardy karonda shrub produces clusters of small, pink-and-white berries that ooze a sticky latex when picked unripe for tangy Indian pickles.
Because raw karonda fruit is intensely sour, cooks often simmer the halved berries with sugar and spices to make a ruby-red relish that mimics cranberry sauce.
In the arid Thar Desert of Rajasthan, the tiny, unripe berry of the leafless ker shrub is cured in brine and sun-dried to preserve it for year-round cooking.
Roughly the size of a caper, the pungent ker fruit is a signature ingredient in traditional Rajasthani desert curries alongside dried sangri beans.
Covered in a thin, buff-colored leathery skin, the Southeast Asian langsat grows in grape-like clusters and conceals translucent segments tasting of sweet grapefruit.
When eating fresh langsat, one must avoid biting into the bitter green seeds nestled inside the juicy arils.
In the Philippines, autumn festivals celebrate the harvest of lanzones, a pale yellow-brown tropical fruit prized for its succulently sweet, translucent flesh.
Peeling the slightly sticky rind of ripe lanzones reveals five or six pearly segments that burst with refreshing, low-acid juice.
Known in English as glue berry due to its viscid, mucilaginous pulp, the green lasora fruit is harvested unripe in northern India for making spicy oil-cured pickles.
Before pickling lasora berries, cooks carefully keep the cap attached to the stem end so the sticky interior does not leak into the spice mixture.
After rubbing off the irritating fuzz covering its bright orange skin, Colombians blend the tart, green-fleshed lulo with water and sugar to make a frothy beverage.
Belonging to the nightshade family, the aromatic lulo fruit features a complex citrus-and-pineapple flavor that rarely survives commercial pasteurization.
A close Amazonian relative of cacao, the woody,ridged macambo pod contains sweet white pulp surrounding large seeds that are roasted into a crunchy snack.
Indigenous communities in Peru eat the aromatic fruit pulp of the macambo fresh from the shell before drying the protein-rich beans over open fires.
Sold in large leafy bunches along tropical highways, the round green mamoncillo has a brittle rind that pops open easily to expose a slippery, apricot-colored pulp.
Because the tangy flesh of the mamoncillo clings tightly to its oversized stone, eaters roll the seed around in their mouths rather than trying to slice the fruit.
When yellow marula fruits drop from the canopy of the African savanna, their turpentine-scented, vitamin-rich pulp quickly ferments in the sun and attracts wildlife.
Beneath the juicy white flesh of the plum-sized marula lies a rock-hard stone containing oil-rich kernels prized in both traditional diets and cosmetics.
Ripening in early May across the river bottoms of the American South, the tiny red mayhaw fruit is harvested from shallow water using nets and tarps.
Too tart and seedy to eat out of hand, wild mayhaw berries are simmered and strained to produce a prized, rose-tinted artisan jelly.
In culinary stone fruits like peaches and mangoes, the succulent, fleshy middle layer between the outer skin and the central pit is botanically termed the mesocarp.
While the mesocarp of a plum is soft and juicy, the corresponding middle layer in a coconut consists of dry, fibrous husk material called coir.
Native to the coastal heathlands of eastern Australia, the low-growing midyim bush produces speckled white berries with a sweet, spicy flavor akin to cinnamon and blueberry.
With its soft skin and tiny edible seeds, the midyim berry was a favorite bushfood of Indigenous Australians and is now gaining popularity in gourmet tarts.
Throughout the winter months in Japan, families gather around heated tables with bowls of seedless mikan, a sweet and loose-skinned mandarin orange.
Because the thin, fragrant peel of a ripe mikan slips off effortlessly by hand, it is one of the most convenient citrus fruits for children's lunchboxes.
Easily recognized by its prominent stem-end neck and deep reddish-orange rind, the minneola tangelo is a cross between a Duncan grapefruit and a Dancy tangerine.
When you slice into a fresh minneola, its thin peel releases a burst of aromatic oil and reveals exceptionally juicy, tart-sweet segments.
The botanical genus momordica encompasses several tropical vines whose warty, gourd-like fruits split open at maturity to display bright red seed arils.
While some momordica fruits are harvested young as bitter culinary vegetables across Asia, others are cultivated for their intensely sweet natural sweeteners.
Harvested from prostrate coastal shrubs in southern Australia, crisp green-and-red muntries berries taste remarkably like spicy, sun-ripened apples.
Historically dried into fruit cakes for winter storage by the Ngarrindjeri people, fresh muntries are now used by modern chefs in chutneys and crumbles.
Often marketed as a honey tangerine due to its rich, nectar-like sweetness, the murcott is a late-season citrus hybrid whose thin rind clings tightly to the flesh.
Because the tender peel of a murcott can be difficult to remove without bruising the juicy interior, many people prefer to cut the fruit into wedges.
The tart yellow and red fruits of the myrobalan, also known as the cherry plum, are prized for making tangy preserves and traditional Georgian sauces.
Horticulturists frequently use the hardy myrobalan tree as rootstock for grafting more delicate commercial plum varieties.
Native to the Andes, the fuzzy orange naranjilla yields a bright green juice with a refreshing flavor reminiscent of both pineapple and lime.
In Ecuador and Colombia, the pulp of the ripe naranjilla is blended with water and sugar to prepare a popular traditional beverage called lulada.
Known across Polynesia as the cheese fruit due to its pungent aroma when ripe, the bumpy green noni has been used in traditional island medicine for centuries.
Despite its bitter taste and strong odor, the noni fruit is widely harvested to produce health tonics and dietary supplements.
Developed by crossing a white grapefruit with an acidless pomelo, the oroblanco offers a sweet, juicy citrus flavor without the typical bitterness of standard grapefruits.
Beneath its thick pale-green rind, the seedless flesh of the oroblanco separates easily into tender, honey-sweet segments.
The large, segmented fruit of the coastal pandanus tree resembles a woody pineapple and consists of fibrous keys that turn bright orange when ripe.
Pacific Islanders boil or roast the starchy fruit segments of the pandanus to create a nutrient-rich paste that sustains communities on coral atolls.
Through the botanical process of parthenocarpy, plants like commercial bananas and seedless watermelons develop full fruits without prior fertilization of the ovules.
Fruit breeders often select for natural parthenocarpy to cultivate consumer-friendly varieties of grapes and citrus that contain no hard seeds.
Indigenous to the rainforests of Borneo, the spiky orange pedalai is a close relative of the jackfruit that splits open easily to reveal sweet, creamy white arils.
Once the soft spines of the pedalai fruit turn yellow-orange, locals harvest the fruit and roast its nutritious seeds much like chestnuts.
With its smooth golden skin streaked with purple, the Andean pepino melon offers a succulent flesh that tastes like a delicate blend of honeydew and cucumber.
Although it is a member of the nightshade family related to tomatoes and eggplants, the sweet pepino is eaten raw as a refreshing dessert fruit.
In botanical classification, a pepo is a specialized berry with a tough, leathery outer rind and fleshy interior, characteristic of pumpkins, cucumbers, and watermelons.
Unlike stone fruits that contain a single hard pit, a pepo encloses numerous flat seeds attached to the inner walls of its central cavity.
A culinary staple of the Brazilian Cerrado, the aromatic yellow pequi fruit must be nibbled with extreme care because a layer of needle-sharp spines surrounds its inner seed.
Cooks simmer the bright golden pulp of the pequi with chicken and rice to impart a rich, cheesy, and slightly citrusy flavor to traditional regional dishes.
Developing from the ovary wall of a flower, the pericarp of a peach is divided into three distinct layers: the fuzzy skin, the juicy flesh, and the hard stone.
In fleshy fruits, the edible pericarp softens and sweetens as it ripens in order to attract animals that will disperse the enclosed seeds.
Harvested during the scorching summer months in South Asia, the tiny dark-purple phalsa berry is prized for its cooling, sweet-tart juice.
Street vendors in India crush fresh phalsa fruits with black salt and sugar to create a refreshing sherbet that helps prevent heatstroke.
Also known as the Suriname cherry, the ribbed crimson pitanga hangs like a miniature lantern from ornamental hedges across South America.
To avoid the resinous aftertaste of unripe fruit, foragers wait until the pitanga turns a deep, glossy maroon and drops into their hands at the slightest touch.
Botanists classify the apple, pear, and quince as a pome, a type of fruit in which a cartilaginous core of seeds is surrounded by crisp, edible floral tissue.
When you eat a pome from the rose family, the sweet flesh you consume actually develops from the flower's receptacle rather than its ovary.
Closely related to the rambutan, the Southeast Asian pulasan features a dark red rind covered in short, blunt nubs rather than long, hair-like spines.
Connoisseurs of tropical produce often prefer the pulasan over the lychee for its exceptionally sweet, translucent flesh that clings tightly to an edible almond-flavored seed.
Native to the arid outback of Australia, the glossy red quandong—often called the desert peach—has been a vital bush tucker food for Indigenous peoples for millennia.
With vitamin C levels twice that of an orange, the tart flesh of the wild quandong is frequently dried for long-term storage or stewed into savory chutneys and pies.
Growing on thorny shrubs throughout tropical Asia and Africa, the dark red ramontchi—commonly known as the governor's plum—has a juicy pulp that balances sweetness with a mild astringency.
Once the plum-like ramontchi softens fully on the branch, its pectin-rich flesh is harvested to make vibrant maroon jellies and fruit wines.
The pear-shaped magenta riberry grows natively in Australian coastal rainforests and offers a distinctive tart flavor accented by warm notes of clove and cinnamon.
Modern chefs pair the spicy-sweet riberry with game meats, cheeses, and decadent chocolate desserts to showcase native Australian bush ingredients.
Nicknamed the lemon meringue pie fruit, the spiky yellow rollinia contains a soft, custard-like white pulp with a bright, citrusy sweetness.
Because the fragile projections on the skin of a ripe rollinia bruise and turn black rapidly after harvest, this Amazonian delicacy is rarely found outside local tropical markets.
Clusters of vibrant scarlet rowan berries brighten mountain forests in autumn, providing essential winter sustenance for migrating thrushes and waxwings.
Although raw rowan fruits are bitter and astringent straight from the tree, freezing and cooking them with sugar transforms them into a tangy jelly traditionally served with venison.
Known in Central Africa as the butterfruit, the oblong violet safou is unusual among fruits for its high concentration of healthy fats and amino acids.
When roasted over hot coals or boiled in salted water, the pale green pulp of the safou softens into a rich, savory spread with the texture of warm avocado.
Immediately recognizable by its reddish-brown, overlapping scales, the Indonesian salak is widely known as snake fruit.
Peeling away the prickly skin of a salak reveals three crisp, yellowish lobes of fruit that combine the sweetness of honey with the tang of pineapple.
Beneath its thick, velvety golden rind, the Southeast Asian santol—or cotton fruit—holds snow-white segments that taste like a tart, floral mangosteen.
In the Philippines, the tangy outer flesh of the santol is grated and simmered in coconut milk with chili peppers to create a rich savory dish called sinantolan.
Named for the spiral arrangement of its thorny leaves, the tropical screwpine produces heavy, compound fruits composed of dozens of bright orange drupes.
Coastal animals and island communities alike rely on the fibrous, sweet-smelling fruit of the screwpine as a durable source of carbohydrates.
A rare intergeneric hybrid between a European pear and a whitebeam tree, the shipova produces small, golden-blushed fruits with smooth, nearly seedless flesh.
Orchardists prize the cold-hardy shipova for its honeyed, aromatic flavor that hints of both ripe pear and tropical mango.
Covered in tough, pyramidal projections, the bowling-ball-sized soncoya is a wild Central American relative of the cherimoya and soursop.
Cracking open the woody rind of a ripe soncoya exposes fibrous, bright orange pulp with an intense tropical aroma reminiscent of mango and papaya.
The small, pear-shaped sorb apple is so astringent when picked that it must undergo bletting—a controlled over-ripening process—before it becomes sweet and palatable.
For centuries across Europe, the fermented juice of the sorb fruit was added to apple cider to clarify the liquid and impart a pleasant tannic bite.
Belonging to the cashew and mango family, the tropical genus Spondias includes popular stone fruits such as the golden ambarella, purple mombin, and yellow hog plum.
Fruits of the Spondias trees are celebrated across the tropics for their crisp, juicy flesh that ranges from refreshingly sour when green to rich and plum-like when fully ripe.
Harvested in Japan's Tokushima Prefecture while its rind is still a vibrant emerald green, the small sudachi citrus is prized for its intensely aromatic, peppery juice.
Rather than being eaten whole as a sweet fruit, the tart sudachi is sliced in half and squeezed over grilled matsutake mushrooms, soba noodles, and fresh sashimi.
Often called the tree tomato, the egg-shaped tamarillo hangs in clusters and features a glossy red or amber skin with a savory, tangy pulp.
Because the skin of the tamarillo is tough and bitter, cooks typically blanch the fruit or slice it in half to scoop out the sweet-tart interior with a spoon.
Recognizable by the prominent neck or knob at its stem end, the tangelo is a juicy citrus hybrid bred by crossing a tangerine with a pomelo or grapefruit.
With its loose, easy-to-peel rind and bright, tangy-sweet flavor, the honeybell tangelo is a winter favorite among citrus enthusiasts.
Native to Borneo, the large round tarap is covered in soft, flexible spines that allow a ripe fruit to be pulled open effortlessly with bare hands.
Inside the thick rind of the tarap, dozens of snow-white arils cluster around a central core, offering a custard-soft texture and a fragrance similar to banana and vanilla.
Also known as the Amazon tree grape, the dark purple uvilla grows in heavy, grape-like clusters on broad-leaved rainforest trees.
Beneath its tough, velvety skin, the uvilla contains a translucent, mucilaginous white pulp with a mild, sweet flavor that locals enjoy fresh or fermented into wine.
Related to citrus fruits, the grape-sized yellow wampee grows in dangling clusters in southern China and bears a resinous, sweet-sour pulp.
Connoisseurs eat the translucent jelly-like flesh of the wampee fresh or simmer the whole berries with sugar to create a soothing syrup for sore throats.
Cultivated in China for over two thousand years, the knobby crimson yangmei—or waxberry—has a juicy, pebbled surface without any outer skin to peel.
Because fresh yangmei berries have a remarkably short shelf life, they are treasured as a fleeting early-summer delicacy or preserved in rice wine and dried snacks.
The yumberry, scientifically known as Myrica rubra, is a bumpy crimson fruit native to eastern Asia that possesses a tart flavor profile reminiscent of pomegranates and cranberries.

Because the delicate flesh of a fresh yumberry spoils within days of harvesting, the exotic fruit is rarely exported whole and is instead commonly processed into antioxidant-rich juices or dried snacks.
